author: mimi1752
quote: Honestly, I wanted to like this game way more than I actually did. And the funny thing is, it looks great. Wolverine looks awesome, the animations are really good, the environments look nice, and the voice acting is genuinely excellent. Some of the characters actually feel convincing just because of how well they’re performed. So at first, I was thinking, “Okay, this is going somewhere.”Then I actually played **** biggest problem for me is how ridiculously easy it is. Wolverine is supposed to be this absolute monster, so obviously you should feel powerful, but here it goes way too far. Most enemies barely feel like enemies. You just run in, slash everything, use a couple of abilities and... that’s it. Fight over. Congratulations, you survived another incredibly dangerous group of guys who apparently forgot how to **** it gets old. Really **** combat looks cool, I’ll give it that, but after a few hours you realize you’re basically doing the same thing over and over again. Fight, walk for a bit, fight again, maybe break some stuff, then fight again. The game keeps giving you new abilities, but somehow they don’t stop the gameplay from feeling repetitive. It’s like they put different toppings on the same pizza and expected me to be excited every **** level design doesn’t help either. This game is so linear. You’re basically being dragged from one objective to the next the entire time. There’s barely any sense of exploration or freedom. You go where the game tells you to go, fight who the game tells you to fight, and move on. At some point I stopped feeling like I was exploring and started feeling like I was being **** then there’s the story, which is probably the most disappointing part because Wolverine could carry such a great story. He’s Wolverine! You have so much material to work with. Instead, we get a pretty standard superhero story that isn’t terrible, but also isn’t especially memorable. There are some decent moments, but nothing that made me think, “Wow, this is an amazing Wolverine story.”So yeah, the game looks good, sounds good, and that’s about where my praise ends. Everything else starts falling apart once the initial excitement wears off. The combat gets repetitive, the game is way too easy, the level design is painfully linear, and the story is just... **** a game about Wolverine, I expected to feel like a terrifying killing machine.Instead, I mostly felt like I was playing a really good-looking hallway.

author: mimi1752
quote: This game is genuinely one of the worst experiences I’ve ever had. Seriously, where do I even start?Let’s start with the combat. The combat is boring as hell. It basically turns into a little box where all you do is dodge attacks, and honestly, it gets boring really fast. You spend the entire fight moving around inside a box, and the worst part is that this is somehow considered the best part of the combat. When you actually attack a character, all you do is press a button. That’s it. There are also dialogue options that can sometimes let you avoid a fight, but even that isn’t anything **** basically, the combat is just moving around in a box and pressing buttons a few times. That’s **** then there’s the story. The story is honestly one of the most overrated things I’ve ever seen in my life. The characters are shallow, the lore is extremely simple, and the plot is genuinely one of the worst I’ve ever seen. I seriously don’t understand how people praise this so **** game is also a visual disaster. And the music doesn’t escape the criticism either. To be fair, the music isn’t THAT bad, but it’s nowhere near as amazing as the fans make it out to be. People talk about it like the soundtrack was created in the ’80s and somehow rediscovered **** somehow, there’s no proper map, the menus are terrible, and there aren’t even languages besides English and Chinese. The comedy is also incredibly cringe most of the **** conclusion, Undertale is honestly one of the most overrated games I’ve ever played. I genuinely don’t understand why people treat it like some masterpiece.
